title: Voice Anti-Spoofing & Audio Watermarking — ASVspoof 5, AudioSeal, WaveVerify

questions.question: A service must identify whether generated speech came from an artificial source. Which defense answers this?
options: Anti-spoofing detection
Speaker diarization
Voice activity detection
Audio provenance signing
questions.explanation: An anti-spoofing detector classifies an incoming clip as real or synthetic/converted, including clips that carry no watermark. A signed manifest records claimed origin; it does not classify the acoustic signal as genuine or synthesized.

questions.question: What distinction does the lesson make between a watermark and a C2PA manifest?
options: A watermark is a model benchmark; C2PA is a speaker encoder
A watermark is a transcript token; C2PA is an audio codec
A watermark detects speech; C2PA estimates an EER
A watermark is perceptual audio data; C2PA is signed metadata
questions.explanation: A watermark is embedded in the perceptual audio signal, while C2PA stores cryptographically signed creation metadata alongside the file. Neither is a transcript or codec: one marks the waveform, and the other signs provenance metadata.

questions.question: Why should production voice systems combine watermarking with a detector?
options: Watermarks cannot identify any generated audio
Aggressive pitch shift can remove watermarks
Signed manifests preserve audio through every re-encode
Detectors work only when a watermark is present
questions.explanation: Pitch shifting can reduce watermark bit recovery below 0.6, so an independent detector is needed when the watermark is removed or unreadable. Anti-spoofing analyzes the audio itself; its detection role complements the watermark rather than depending on it.

questions.question: What information can AudioSeal place in its documented payload?
options: A complete C2PA manifest inside every frame
A 16-bit model, time, or user identifier
A 1,000-token audio codec sequence
A 32-byte transcript and speaker embedding
questions.explanation: AudioSeal carries a compact 16-bit payload, or two bytes, suitable for identifiers such as model, time, or user codes. Thirty-two bytes is 256 bits, far larger than the documented payload and not a complete signed manifest.

questions.question: A TTS service needs an authenticity layer that remains detectable after common compression. What integration matches the lesson?
options: Use energy VAD as the watermark verifier
Embed AudioSeal and run its detector in CI
Sign C2PA metadata and skip all audio detection
Add a transcript tag after the WAV file is uploaded
questions.explanation: The production path embeds AudioSeal and runs its detector in CI so the watermark can be checked after common compression tests. The lesson notes re-encoding can strip metadata, so provenance signing does not replace the perceptual watermark and detector.

questions.question: An AASIST detector performs well on ASVspoof LA but poorly on phone audio. What is the next step?
options: Keep the benchmark threshold unchanged in production
Calibrate and evaluate it on the target domain
Replace detection with a watermark lookup alone
Report its benchmark result as real-world accuracy
questions.explanation: Good ASVspoof benchmark performance can overfit its recording conditions; calibrate and evaluate the detector on the phone-audio domain before deployment. The benchmark score alone does not establish error rates under a different channel and noise distribution.
